analysis.one_liner: Bars Medicare patients from owing more than Medicare's charge limit and forces doctors to refund overcharges.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it died in House subcommittees when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare already caps what nonparticipating doctors may charge seniors, but patients were still being billed above that limit. This bill would have made clear that beneficiaries owe nothing above the cap, required doctors to refund excess charges within 30 days, threatened sanctions against doctors who repeatedly overbill, and told patients what the cap is and that refunds are available. It was referred to two House committees and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who use doctors that do not participate in Medicare. They would no longer be legally liable for charges above Medicare's limiting charge, would get their money back if overcharged, and would receive written notice of their rights.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare seniors billed above the cap

how_it_helps.text: The bill states that no Medicare beneficiary may be liable for amounts a nonparticipating physician bills above the limiting charge, retroactive to services on or after January 1, 1991.

Physicians must refund excess charges within 30 days of notice, or within 15 days after losing an appeal, and the Secretary may sanction doctors who knowingly and repeatedly overbill or fail to refund on time.

Medicare carriers must screen nonparticipating physicians' claims before payment and notify doctors of the refund requirement, and beneficiaries must receive written notice of the charge limit and their refund rights.

analysis.who_pays: Nonparticipating physicians who bill above Medicare's limit would lose that revenue and face sanctions for repeat overbilling; Medicare carriers would take on new prepayment screening and notice duties, a cost ultimately carried by the Medicare program.

drawbacks.text: The prepayment screening requirement adds administrative work for Medicare carriers and physicians, and processing could slow payments for nonparticipating doctors' services.
The bill applies retroactively to services furnished on or after January 1, 1991, meaning physicians could owe refunds for care billed well before the law passed.
Sanctions for 'knowing and willful' repeated overbilling invite disputes over a physician's intent, which could mean appeals and enforcement costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For beneficiaries, the direct benefit is real but targeted: it enforces an existing cap rather than creating a new one, so the main gain is refunding money seniors were wrongly billed and deterring repeat overchargers. The costs — carrier screening work, physician paperwork, and a retroactive effective date that reaches back over a year — are modest but not trivial. On balance it shifts money and risk from seniors to the small share of doctors billing above the cap.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees on the day it was introduced, then passed to their health subcommittees, where it sat with no hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim McDermott introduced the bill on May 7, 1992, with four original cosponsors (three Democrats and one Republican).
The same day, the House referred it jointly to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees.
Within two weeks it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health and the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and the Environment.
No further action was recorded, and the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nonparticipating physicians who billed above Medicare's charge limit kept doing so without a mandatory refund obligation or sanctions, and Medicare beneficiaries continued to absorb excess charges. With only four cosponsors and no committee action, the bill never came close to a floor vote, so there was no visible bloc that had to defeat it.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and three of four cosponsors were Democrats, with one Republican cosponsor, and no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of broader support or opposition was never tested.

industries.note: Doctors outside Medicare's participation agreement could bill patients above Medicare's limiting charge and keep the excess. The bill would have made patients legally owe nothing above the cap, forced refunds within 30 days, and authorized sanctions for repeat overbilling, cutting off that revenue.

Carriers would gain a new enforcement role — screening nonparticipating physicians' claims before payment and notifying doctors of refund obligations — but that is added administrative work with no new revenue, so gains and burdens roughly offset.
